How this book matches your exam. IB Business Management (guide first assessed in 2024) has five units: 1 Introduction to business management, 2 Human resource management, 3 Finance and accounts, 4 Marketing, 5 Operations management, plus the business management toolkit. It is assessed as follows:

  • Paper 1 (pre-released statement, unseen case study): 1h30, 30 marks; 35% at SL, 25% at HL;
  • Paper 2 (quantitative, unseen stimulus): SL 1h30, 40 marks, 35%; HL 1h45, 50 marks, 30%;
  • Paper 3 (HL only, a social enterprise): 1h15, 25 marks, 25%;
  • Business research project (IA): at most 1800 words, 25 marks, using one key concept (change, creativity, ethics or sustainability); 30% at SL, 20% at HL.

This book covers Unit 1 (1.1–1.6): the nature of business, types of organisations, objectives, stakeholders, the external environment, and growth and evolution (including HL multinational companies). The mark allocations are our own guides, written in the style of IB markschemes.

Unit 1 of 10: What Is a Business?

Key ideas

  • A business combines resources (the factors of production) to produce goods or services that meet people's needs and wants.
  • The four factors of production:
  • land (natural resources);
  • labour (human effort);
  • capital (machinery and equipment);
  • enterprise (the entrepreneur who organises the others and takes risks).
  • Business functions: human resources, finance and accounts, marketing, and operations. They are interdependent: a decision in one affects the others.

Worked examples

Example 1: a café uses land (premises), labour (baristas), capital (coffee machines) and enterprise (the owner).

Example 2: marketing plans a promotion → operations must produce more → finance must fund the extra stock → HR may need to hire temporary staff.

Example 3: a business adds value when the selling price exceeds the cost of its bought-in materials.

10-mark exam-style question

Mala's Bakery is a small bakery in Pune that sells bread and cakes.

(a) Define the term "factors of production". [2]

(b) Identify one example of each factor of production for Mala's Bakery. [4]

(c) Explain how a decision to open a second shop would affect two business functions. [4]

Answers:

  • (a) The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise (A2).
  • (b) Land: the shop site; labour: the bakers; capital: the ovens; enterprise: Mala, who takes the risk (A4).
  • (c) Finance: Mala needs funds for the premises and equipment, for example a loan (R2). HR: she must recruit and train new staff to run the second shop (R2).

Common mistakes

  1. Defining capital as "money" only.
  2. Giving generic examples not linked to the case.
  3. Treating business functions as separate, unrelated departments.
  4. Mixing up enterprise and labour.
  5. Not applying the answer to the business named.

Quick recall

  1. Name the four factors of production.
  2. What is enterprise?
  3. Name the four business functions.
  4. What does "interdependent" mean?
  5. What is added value?

Answers: 1) Land, labour, capital, enterprise. 2) Organising the other factors and taking risks. 3) HR, finance, marketing, operations. 4) A decision in one function affects the others. 5) The price minus the cost of bought-in materials.
